title: Could A Robot Tax Win the War on Poverty?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore universal basic income (UBI), using Andrew Yang's "Freedom Dividend" proposal of $1,000 a month to every adult as the central example. They cover the case for replacing means-tested safety-net programs, the push to fund UBI through a value-added tax, a robot tax, and carbon taxes, and the pros (buffer for health, education, entrepreneurship, better bargaining power for workers) and cons (cost, inflation, reduced work hours, incentives around children). They also cover history (Milton Friedman's negative income tax, Nixon's Family Assistance Plan, Keynes's 1930 leisure prediction, Martin Luther King's support), trial programs (Kenya cash transfers, Stockton pilot funded by Chris Hughes, Alaska Permanent Fund), and the earned income tax credit. The episode closes with a listener mail from Greg Bell about how the show influenced his choices.

segments.title: Tour postponement and opening banter
segments.summary: Opening note about postponed tour dates due to coronavirus, then the hosts introduce universal basic income and their initial reactions to it.

segments.title: What universal basic income is and the flat tax comparison
segments.summary: The hosts define UBI as a no-strings payment to every adult, using Andrew Yang's $1,000 a month Freedom Dividend. They compare it with a flat tax, which they describe as regressive, and question whether UBI could replace existing safety-net programs for people who cannot work.

segments.title: Automation, robots and the payroll tax problem
segments.summary: The hosts discuss job loss from automation, the estimate that about 30 percent of working Americans could lose jobs to robots, and how payroll and unemployment taxes that fund safety nets shrink as labor is automated. They raise Bill Gates's robot tax idea and the difficulty of retraining workers.

segments.title: Inequality and the moral case for basic income
segments.summary: The hosts argue that US poverty and inequality have persisted since World War Two and that the country has a moral obligation to provide for its citizens. They note that Martin Luther King Jr. championed a similar idea.

segments.title: Pros of UBI: individual payments, health, education and bargaining power
segments.summary: The hosts describe benefits: payments go to each individual, which helps unpaid caregivers; a financial buffer lets people focus on health, education, or starting businesses; and workers could negotiate better wages and conditions. They also mention Chris Hughes's Stockton pilot and the need for catastrophic health insurance.

segments.title: Kenya cash experiment and libertarian and conservative support
segments.summary: The hosts describe a Kenya direct-cash experiment in which recipients used money for food and small businesses. They also explain why libertarians and some conservatives like UBI, including Charles Murray's argument that it could replace the welfare state and cost less than current programs.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Sponsor break before the critiques section.

segments.title: Criticisms: cost, inflation, work disincentives
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the cost estimate of about $2.3 trillion a year, concerns that people would stop working or spend the money unwisely, the fear of inflation from increased demand, and the disincentive effects of existing welfare programs.

segments.title: Paying for UBI: VAT, robot tax, carbon tax and history
segments.summary: The hosts explain how a value-added tax works and why Yang proposed one, with necessities exempted. They also cover robot taxes, carbon taxes, and history: Milton Friedman's negative income tax, Nixon's Family Assistance Plan with its work requirement, and the earned income tax credit. They close by discussing Keynes's leisure prediction and the timing of automation.

segments.title: Child incentives and closing thoughts on UBI
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether UBI or the earned income tax credit could encourage people to have children, and how a family could pool payments. They end by saying they are not fully sold on UBI and discuss personal volunteering and donation.

segments.title: Listener mail from Greg Bell
segments.summary: Chuck reads a listener mail from Greg Bell, who says the show led him to study history and to become an educator at the Booth Western Art Museum. Chuck also mentions a University of Georgia alumni talk at a whiskey distillery.
